# A Map of a Single Afternoon

I bought the notebook on a Tuesday at a stationery shop near the south entrance to the railway station. It was dark green, bound in cloth, with a pale elastic band holding it shut. The pages were blank. Not lined, not squared, not decorated with quotations about mountains or seasons—just blank paper, generous and slightly yellowed at the edges.

I had carried it home under my arm and placed it on the kitchen table, where it remained for three weeks.

The idea was to fill it. That was all. No obligation to make it beautiful, no demand that it become useful. I simply wanted to put something into those empty pages before the year became another sealed box of things postponed. I had been feeling, though I would not have admitted it to anyone, as though I were watching life through a window that had grown slightly too clean. Everything beyond the glass looked vivid. Everything inside it had become familiar to the point of disappearance.

So I decided to take a walk.

Not a walk with a destination. That was important. A walk to the bakery would have been an errand. A walk to the park would have been exercise. I wanted a walk that could end anywhere, or continue after it had apparently ended, or double back without efficiency. I wanted to give the day room to surprise me.

At eight in the morning, I left the notebook at home. This seemed contradictory to the purpose of the walk, but I trusted the contradiction. I had learned that some instructions are most useful once forgotten.

The city was already awake, though reluctantly. Delivery bicycles stood in crooked rows outside the grocery. A man in a blue apron hosed down the pavement in front of the bakery. His hose made a bright metallic sound, and the water ran into the gutter in a quick, brown ribbon. Two swallows were investigating the awning above the bakery door. They touched down, flew up, touched down again. Their urgency looked almost mathematical.

Inside, the smell of warm bread overwhelmed everything else. Butter, yeast, toasted flour, and beneath them something darker, like the memory of a fire that had gone out but left its scent in the walls.

I bought a coffee and a roll with sesame seeds. The woman behind the counter asked whether I wanted the cup warmed.

“I didn’t know that was an option,” I said.

“It’s not,” she said. “But if you want it, I can warm the cup.”

I said yes.

She held the empty cup beneath a hot tap for a few seconds, dried it with a cloth, and handed it to me. The coffee was no better than it had been in an unwarmed cup. The bread was no better. Yet the gesture stayed with me, not as wisdom but as an event. Someone had offered me a tiny unnecessary kindness, and I had accepted it without asking what it meant.

Outside, I passed a bench with one loose screw. The screw lay in the morning light like a fallen comma. I picked it up. It was longer than it looked, the threads sharp and dark with dust. For a moment I wondered who had tightened it there, who had sat on that bench, and why the screw was now separated from the thing it belonged to.

Then I put it in my coat pocket and kept walking.

The first thing I noticed was how much of the city was designed for bodies. A low wall beside a doorway, perhaps for a bicycle or a pram. A stone worn smooth at the edge of a step, polished by generations of feet. A doorway narrowed because a door had once opened inward. Even the fire escapes seemed to have been built with a kind of practical tenderness, their ladders descending into narrow yards where washing was always hanging.

We tend to speak of buildings as if they were ideas: stone, glass, steel, concrete. But a city is mostly the accumulated results of human inconvenience. It is steps built for tired knees. Cornices built to carry rain away from those entering. Balconies built for people who wanted to stand outside without becoming completely outside. A city is a record of what people have needed while pretending they needed nothing.

Near the river, I found a laundromat with six machines visible through the window. Only two were running. Behind one of them, a woman waited with a red plastic basket balanced on her hip. She watched the drum turn with the expression of someone supervising a slow journey.

I stood for a while, pretending to read the notices on the door.

One announced that the lost-property box would be emptied every Friday. Another offered advice about a stain that might not come out. The window reflected the street behind me: bicycles, clouds, the pale underside of a plane passing overhead. On the glass, written in soap, someone had drawn a square and then the word *almost*.

I entered.

The woman with the basket looked up. The machines shook and clicked in alternating rhythms. One sounded like a boot being dragged across gravel. The other sounded like applause heard from a great distance.

“I can help you,” she said, though she had no reason to think I needed help.

“I’m only looking.”

“That’s allowed,” she said.

The lost-property box contained one black glove, two silver buttons, a child’s bracelet, a receipt, and a single orange. This was not a mystery I was obligated to solve. The glove had a hole in the palm. The buttons were dull. The bracelet had a faded blue thread tied around its clasp. The receipt was from a hardware store and gave no useful information. The orange was beginning to soften.

I looked at each object for longer than was reasonable.

The glove had probably been lost by someone whose hand was still warm. The buttons had once held two pieces of fabric together. The bracelet had belonged to an owner who might have been a child, or might have been someone who liked the color blue. The orange had probably rolled from someone’s pocket, or fallen from a bag, or been offered and rejected.

None of these thoughts produced knowledge. They were only possibilities, and the mind is so eager to complete a story that it will turn a button into a tragedy if given half a chance.

Still, the objects had changed under attention. The glove was no longer empty. The orange was no longer merely fruit. They had entered the temporary republic of things without owners.

When I left the laundromat, the woman was still watching her machine. The city had not revealed a secret. It had simply shown me the ordinary world at close range.

The rain began as a warning.

A drop struck the awning above a closed shop, then another, then ten. People opened umbrellas with small, practiced flicks. The pavement darkened almost immediately. The air acquired the scent of mineral dust and wet leaves. Traffic sounds softened, and the city seemed to lower its voice.

Under the awnings, people gathered without forming a crowd. A delivery rider stood beside a man holding a folder. A woman in a red coat checked her phone while an older man studied the rain as if it were a theatrical performance.

Rain changes the proportions of a street. Dry, the street is a route. Wet, it becomes a collection of reflections. The red traffic light floated on a puddle. A yellow building leaned in a silver patch. Faces appeared, stretched and broken, in the polished surface of a parked car.

For a few minutes, the city seemed to contain a second version of itself, more unstable and more honest. You could see the sky without looking up. You could see the height of a building without seeing the building. The rain did not make the world more beautiful. It made the world harder to reduce to one description.

I stood beneath an awning and watched a gutter carry leaves toward the drain. A child ran past with her arms lifted, her face tilted upward. Her mother called her name, not sternly, but with the particular tone that means *come back into the world now*.

The child ignored her.

I understood the temptation.

In the middle of the afternoon, I found myself at the entrance of a small museum I had never noticed. Its sign read **Municipal History, Infrastructure, and Useful Machines**. The windows displayed an old streetlamp, a section of pavement, a rusted manhole cover, and a machine once used to grind coffee.

The exhibit had been arranged with less ceremony than the word *museum* usually demanded. A brass plaque explained that the streetlamp had been installed in 1938 and removed in 1981. Another plaque explained that the pavement came from a warehouse demolished to make room for the present road.

The most interesting object was an enormous brass valve.

It stood on a low wooden platform, polished by visitors’ hands. The plaque beside it said that water once traveled beneath the city through pipes like this, and that the valve allowed workers to regulate the flow.

A child asked her father why the valve was so shiny.

“People touch it,” he said.

She nodded, as if this were a perfectly satisfactory answer.

I touched it too. The brass was warm from the nearby radiators. It was not beautiful in the usual way. It had dents, scratches, and a greenish stain near one edge. But it had survived long enough to become a destination, and now people came specifically to lay their palms against it.

I thought about how history is often presented as a procession of famous events. War. Revolution. Genius. Discovery. But most history is made from things like this: a valve, a lamp, a strip of pavement. Someone carried a heavy object. Someone tightened a bolt. Someone repaired a thing so ordinary that no one thought to describe it afterward.

The museum was nearly empty. In a glass case lay a ceramic cup with a chip in its handle. The cup had belonged to a clerk named Peter Venn, who worked in the municipal office for thirty-one years. The display card gave his dates, the year he started work, and the year he died. It did not say what his voice sounded like, or what he ate for lunch, or whether he had a preferred chair.

I stared at the dates as though the cup might be persuaded to say more.

It did not.

Yet the dates had a different weight after the cup. They no longer looked like small brackets surrounding a blank. They looked like two points of pressure on a sheet of paper, pressing from opposite sides.

Outside, the rain had stopped. The clouds were breaking apart, and sunlight fell through them in long, pale columns. The wet pavement held the light better than the dry stone.

I found a record shop that afternoon, tucked between a tailor and a business that repaired radios but had no sign. Inside, the walls were covered in records in plastic sleeves. A man sat behind the counter reading a newspaper. The newspaper was at least a decade old. He did not look up when I entered.

I put on a pair of headphones connected to a listening station. The first record I chose had a title I did not recognize. A woman’s voice sang about a train that arrived after midnight. The melody was simple, almost too simple to hold attention. But as I listened, I began to notice the small imperfections: the breath before one line, the scrape of a chair, a harmony that came in half a second late and somehow made the whole song feel trustworthy.

The train in the song traveled through places I knew. A street with a clock tower. A hotel with a blue sign. A platform where the lamps were too bright. The singer did not describe these places. She simply passed through them, and the melody made them available to anyone willing to listen.

This is one of the wonders of old recordings: they preserve a kind of presence without preserving the person. You can hear the air around a voice. You can hear the room. You can hear the moment before the voice begins, when the singer is still deciding to sing.

I bought the record. I could not have told anyone what it was about. I could only say that I had wanted to bring the voice home.

Outside, the rain had left the city shining in fragments. Bicycle frames. Door handles. A row of metal shutters. The air smelled washed and newly cool. People moved quickly, as if the rain had made them late for something.

On a bench near the park, I found a small brass key.

It was attached to nothing. No tag, no key ring, no recognizable fob. The key was warm, as though someone had been holding it just before letting it go. I sat on the bench and turned it over.

A key is an invitation with a very small shape. It promises access, but only to someone who knows where the lock is. It is useless without a door. It is meaningful only in relation to absence.

I thought of all the keys I had lost and never lost. The key to a childhood home. The key to a bicycle. The key I had once carried for years after the lock had been changed. We imagine objects as independent things, but most of them are verbs in disguise. A key opens. A cup holds. A book carries. A map directs. A letter asks. A photograph keeps.

The brass key in my hand asked nothing of me. It did not belong to my life. That was why I could look at it so freely.

The park was not large. It had a gravel path, a pond, a patch of grass where dogs were permitted, and a row of plane trees whose bark had peeled away in irregular patches. An old man sat on a bench feeding pigeons from a paper bag.

“Do they have names?” I asked.

He looked at me. “Which ones?”

“The pigeons.”

“Some do,” he said.

He pointed toward a pigeon with one wing slightly raised. “That one is called Mr. Difficult.”

“Why?”

“Because he never comes when I call him.”

The pigeon walked a few steps and flew onto the roof of a kiosk.

I laughed, and the old man smiled, though he did not seem surprised. He returned to the paper bag and offered a piece of bread to a pigeon who immediately took it.

“You know,” he said, “the birds don’t care whether I call them by name. They care whether I have bread.”

I considered this.

It was a modest philosophy, but perhaps modest philosophies are the ones most often tested by experience. We want the world to recognize our names, our intentions, our private meanings. We want to believe that the objects around us are waiting to be interpreted correctly. But the pigeon cared about bread. The coffee cup cared about warmth. The rain cared about the shape of the roof.

The world did not refuse meaning. It simply refused to guarantee that our meanings would be returned to us.

On the hill above the river, the city opened out beneath me. From there, the buildings looked less like separate structures and more like layers of sediment. Old roofs, new towers, chimneys, cranes, water tanks, glass panels reflecting clouds. The river divided the city and joined it at the same time, carrying the pale afternoon toward the sea.

A city is always a temporary arrangement. Every building is a decision made by someone who believed it would last. Every street is a promise about how people would move through a particular patch of ground. The hill showed me how those promises overlapped. A warehouse became apartments. A field became a road. A road became a shopping street. A shopping street became a place where someone sold flowers out of a metal bucket.

Nothing stays still, but nothing disappears completely. The city is full of ghosts that have not been frightened away. They remain in the height of a doorway, in the angle of a wall, in the place where a tree once stood and left a circle of dry earth.

The sun began to set, turning the windows orange, then red, then silver. The river held the light. Boats moved slowly across it, their wakes spreading outward and dissolving.

I opened the notebook.

The first page contained a list of things I had seen:

*Coffee cup, warmed but no better.*

*Loose screw.*

*Brass valve.*

*Key without a door.*

*Pigeon named Mr. Difficult.*

*Orange in lost property.*

*Woman’s voice singing about midnight trains.*

I did not know what these things meant together. That was reassuring. I had feared the notebook would demand a conclusion, that every observation would have to become part of a larger argument. Instead, the list made room for incompletion.

I wrote a little more.

A patch of pavement shining after rain.

A child running with her face turned upward.

The word *almost* written in soap.

A man reading a newspaper that had been old when he was young.

The smell of bread in a narrow street.

A clockmaker’s shop, open late, with a single lamp burning above the door.

I wrote until the handwriting became less like handwriting and more like a pattern. I did not worry about the pattern. It was enough that the day had entered the paper.

On the walk back, I passed the bakery, now closed. The blue-aproned man had gone home. The pavement was dry. The swallows were gone, or hidden, or somewhere above the clouds. The bench remained, and the loose screw remained in my pocket, though I had no intention of returning it.

At the river, I saw someone standing at the railing. She held a folded piece of paper in both hands. For a moment I thought she might throw it into the water. Instead, she opened it, read it, and put it back in her coat.

Maybe it was a letter. Maybe it was a shopping list. Maybe it was a page torn from a book. I would never know, and the not-knowing no longer felt like failure.

I had spent years believing that attention was a kind of extraction. I wanted to look at the world and take from it: a lesson, a story, an image that would become mine. I wanted to know the ending before the journey began. I wanted the ordinary to confess that it was ordinary.

But the city offered no such confession. It remained a city, made of people going about their business, carrying their invisible lives from one place to another. The baker had opened his shop. The woman had washed her clothes. The man had read his newspaper. The old man had fed the pigeons. The child had run into the rain. The stranger had read her letter.

Their lives were not illustrations for mine.

This was, perhaps, the most comforting thing I had discovered all day.

The notebook did not contain a revelation. It contained a record of not being elsewhere. That was enough. I closed it, tied the elastic band around it, and watched the last light leave the river.

The city did not become new. I had not become someone who paid attention in an exceptional way. There would be other days when I would walk through streets without seeing them, when I would eat a meal without tasting it, when I would answer a question while thinking about something else. I would forget the loose screw. I would misplace the brass key. I would fail to notice that the rain had begun until my shoes were wet.

But now I had evidence that such days could be interrupted.

I had seen the valve polished by hands. The cup warmed for no reason. The pigeons who cared only about bread. The word *almost* written on a laundromat window by someone who might have meant it as a joke, or a warning, or an explanation.

The evening came, and the windows brightened one by one.

I walked home carrying no answer, only the feeling that the world had been there all along, waiting not to be solved but to be entered.

samples.result:
# In Praise of Getting Lost

There is a particular quiet that arrives when a person realizes they are lost. The street you expected is not there. The shop on the corner has closed, moved, or apparently never existed. Your phone offers to help, but for a moment you resist it. For a few seconds, maybe a minute, the world is larger than your plans. You are standing in the wrong place, and the wrong place has a view.

I remember getting lost for the first time in a city I thought I knew. I was looking for a small public garden whose entrance I had seen on a map. I walked confidently for several blocks, then less confidently, and finally stopped beneath a tree while a bus passed with the unhurried indifference of public transport. I had forgotten the name of the street. More importantly, I had forgotten why I thought I knew the way. The garden was still there, somewhere, but my certainty had collapsed before I arrived. I found it eventually by asking someone. The journey took twenty minutes longer than it should have. I never forgot the embarrassment, but I also remember noticing things on the wrong street: a bakery with open doors, a cat asleep on a windowsill, a patch of sunlight falling across an old wall. Those things did not appear on the map. They would not have appeared in the version of the walk that went perfectly.

A map is one of civilization’s great acts of confidence. It takes a landscape full of infinite detail and compresses it into lines, symbols, colors, and distances. It declares that the territory can be held still long enough to be described. It promises that somewhere, in offices or institutions or the collective imagination, there is a correct version of where things are. Most of the time, the promise is useful. We need to know which bridge crosses the river, where the train station is, whether the road continues beyond the next bend. But a map is also an argument. It tells us which features matter, which connections deserve emphasis, and which spaces may safely be left blank. It is not a failure of a map to omit the smell of rain on pavement, but it is a failure if we forget that it has omitted them.

Childhood maps are often wonderfully inaccurate. Mine included a swimming pool that was at least three blocks from its actual location, a railway line that disappeared behind a hedge, and a mysterious path I had invented to avoid walking past a house where someone had once said something unkind. Distances were adjusted according to feeling rather than measurement. A destination that took twenty minutes to reach might be drawn close if I liked it; a place I disliked could be pushed toward the edge of the page. These maps were useless for navigation and excellent for memory. They recorded not only where I thought things were, but what I believed about them.

We tend to imagine that maps became more accurate before they became more personal. Certainly, modern maps have become more detailed, more searchable, and more responsive to our particular intentions. They can show the shortest route, the safest route, the route with a library, the route avoiding hills, the route that passes a particular kind of coffee shop. We can ask them to favor parks or avoid motorways. A contemporary map is less a picture of the territory than a set of suggestions about how to move through it. That is valuable. It is also a little unsettling. The map no longer simply tells us where we are. It tells us where we ought to go.

Before printed directions, getting lost was an ordinary part of moving through the world. People traveled by landmarks, stories, and the knowledge of locals. A guide might say that you could not miss a certain place, although it lay beyond two rivers and a stand of trees. A sign might point toward a village whose name most travelers had never heard. In unfamiliar places, people accepted a level of uncertainty that now feels excessive, even though their practical knowledge was often considerable. They knew how to read weather, seasons, animal behavior, the slope of the ground, and the changing color of the sky. They could be lost geographically without being helpless.

This does not mean that older travelers were automatically wise. Someone who was lost could still be exhausted, frightened, or late. Nor was every old map a masterpiece of mystery, filled with imaginative monsters and distant countries drawn from rumor. But older maps often admitted more about the limits of their knowledge. A blank region might remain blank. A coastline could fade into decorative uncertainty. The map did not always pretend that its information was equally trustworthy everywhere. In that respect, it occasionally offered a lesson we have since struggled to learn: not every space needs to be occupied by a label.

A wrong turn is one of the oldest forms of unplanned travel. It has produced some of the best stories precisely because nobody chose it. The person who accidentally enters a side street discovers a courtyard, a language lesson, an argument about a statue, or a view that becomes the reason they remember the entire trip. The famous discovery is usually presented as the work of a person who knew exactly what they were looking for, but many discoveries begin with a small failure of navigation. We call it a detour, as if the deviation were simply a technical matter of distance. Sometimes it is. Most of the time, a detour changes the route and the person taking it.

Not every wrong turn is a gift. Some are simply wrong. A missed train can mean a missed appointment, a missed exit can mean hours of delay, and a mistaken assumption about a neighborhood can have consequences that have nothing to the romance of wandering. The point is not that inconvenience is valuable in itself. The point is that the shortest path is not the only path capable of producing knowledge. Efficiency answers the question, “How do I get there?” It does not answer the questions that appear when the original route disappears.

The optimized world has little patience for this. Every journey is evaluated by duration, fuel consumption, energy expenditure, and the number of interruptions required. The fastest route is presented as the obvious one, even when the slower road passes a market, a reservoir, or a village with an excellent bakery. A navigation system can know that a street is pleasant before nine in the morning and congested afterward, but it cannot know that you have been sitting in an office for six hours and need to see a horizon. It can optimize for arrival while missing the journey entirely.

There is a deeper problem with this kind of optimization. When every route is judged by its usefulness, places that serve no immediate purpose become difficult to justify. A street with no destination at its end is suspicious. A park is good if it improves health, increases property value, or provides a pleasant view. A person who takes a walk without a destination may be assumed to be wasting time, though walking may be the activity that makes the rest of life possible. Efficiency is valuable. It becomes dangerous when it pretends to be the only form of value.

Getting lost also reveals how much our sense of direction depends on stories. We do not experience space as a blank grid. We experience it through memory and expectation. A shortcut is not merely a line between two points; it is the remembered path taken with someone, the route avoided because of a storm, the way home from a school where we once felt afraid. When those stories change, our physical surroundings can become strange. A familiar building is replaced. A shop becomes a bank. A tree that once marked the turning point is cut down. The city is still there, but the map inside the mind has failed to keep up.

This is one reason people sometimes become disoriented in places they have visited many times. The body remembers a route that no longer exists. The mind insists on a landmark that has vanished. We are not simply bad at directions; we are responding to an older arrangement of the world. A person who has relied on a particular street for years may feel genuinely lost when a construction fence blocks it, even if another route is perfectly available. Being lost can be a form of grief for a place that no longer exists.

The same is true of cities remembered through other people. A grandmother’s route to the bus stop may include a bakery that has since become an office block. A childhood shortcut may run through a field now covered by houses. The person who tells the story is not only giving directions. They are offering access to a version of the world that exists in memory. To be asked for help is therefore to be asked, “Can you show me how your world connects to mine?” The answer may come in the form of a detailed explanation, or it may be a simple gesture toward a steeple, a bridge, a particular tree, or a clock tower.

Strangers are unexpectedly good at this. They know the scale of the neighborhood in a way that a printed map cannot. They know which door sticks in wet weather, which crossing has no signal, where the pavement becomes muddy after rain, and which shortcut is only a shortcut for someone with long legs. Their instructions are full of practical wisdom. “Go past the place with the blue shutters.” “Take the next street after the church.” “You’ll see it when the road bends toward the hills.” These are not coordinates. They are relationships between things, and relationships are what memory is made of.

The person who asks for directions must also relinquish a little pride. A traveler with a carefully planned itinerary can usually find the answer alone, even if it takes longer. A lost person must admit that the local knowledge of a stranger is more useful than their own. That admission is often easier when the stakes are small. It becomes harder when the lostness is more serious: when someone has no safe place to return to, when a border has closed behind them, when the language on the signs is unfamiliar, when the map is not merely inaccurate but actively misleading.

We should therefore distinguish between the freedom to wander and the condition of being stranded. Most of us have the privilege of choosing unfamiliarity. We can take a wrong turn and expect to recover. We can miss a train and know that another will come. We can carry a charged phone, identification, money, and a sense of how to ask for help. Others do not have that luxury. For them, uncertainty is not a recreational state. It can mean danger, exploitation, deportation, violence, or simply the absence of any place where one is welcome. To praise getting lost is not to romanticize the experience of everyone who says they are lost. It is to notice that a map and a welcome are not the same thing.

There is also a danger in making novelty itself a goal. Some people travel only to collect experiences, and some experiences are exhausted quickly. A person can visit many places and remain remarkably uninterested in them. They may move from landmark to landmark, photograph each one, and return home with an album full of evidence that they have been elsewhere. The difficulty is not staying in one place. It is becoming unable to be present in any place. A new street is not necessarily an escape from routine if the person is carrying routine everywhere with them.

To get lost deliberately, then, is to become temporarily less goal-shaped. It is a practice of attention. Instead of asking only where the destination is, one can ask what is on the corner, why the street curves that way, which direction the wind is coming from, what the buildings are made of, and who might have chosen the names on them. These questions do not help a person arrive more quickly. They make arrival less important for a while.

The practice can begin on an ordinary walk. Leave the usual route at the next safe intersection. Walk without checking the phone for a few minutes. Choose a street because it looks interesting rather than because it is efficient. Sit on a bench with no purpose beyond sitting. Learn the name of a tree. Notice the difference between a street that is busy because people must pass through it and one that is busy because people have decided to stay. These are small acts, but they loosen the grip of habit. They restore the sense that the built environment is not a machine designed to move us from one predetermined point to another.

Maps are especially useful when they help us notice what we would otherwise overlook. A transit map can show the shape of a city’s history, which lines were built first, where the stations cluster, and how neighborhoods are connected or separated. A weather map can turn an apparently shapeless sky into patterns of pressure and wind. Even a map of a park can teach us to see a landscape as a set of designed relationships rather than an undifferentiated green space. The problem is not the map. It is the belief that the map is complete.

Every person carries a private cartography. It includes the grocery store where a friend first told them some difficult news, the corner where they once waited in the rain, the bench from which a child watched a procession, the shortcut that makes them feel briefly brave. Some of these locations are marked on public maps. None of them are marked in the ordinary sense. A favorite place is not primarily a coordinate. It is a relationship between a place and a version of oneself who has existed there.

This is why a city can be accurately mapped and still be unknown. A person may know all the street names and have no idea where to find a quiet place to think. They may know how to reach the center and not how to reach the river. They may possess perfect directions to a friend’s house and have no memory of the conversation that took place there. Official geography is not the whole geography of a life. The missing parts are often the parts that make us willing to return.

Getting lost with other people adds another dimension. Children are frequently better at it than adults because they have not yet learned to treat every detour as an error. A child may insist on inspecting a stick, a beetle, a puddle, or a patch of grass that everyone else would prefer to ignore. The group slows down. An adult becomes impatient. Eventually, the child’s delay turns out to have involved something worth seeing. This does not mean children should be required to lead every expedition. It means that their willingness to stop can interrupt the adult obsession with progress.

Travel with other people also reveals how differently people understand a destination. One person may care about the scenery, another about arriving on time, another about finding a particular meal, and another about seeing an old friend. When a route changes, these priorities are exposed. The detour is inconvenient for one person and liberating for another. A shared journey can survive the disruption, or it can become a series of private complaints. The lostness is the same; the meaning assigned to it is not.

The modern world makes it increasingly difficult to be lost, and sometimes that is a good thing. Emergency services need accurate addresses. Airports need clear signs. Search-and-rescue teams need maps. There is no virtue in failing to read a warning sign or refusing directions when a person is exhausted, vulnerable, or far from home. The celebration of wandering should never become an argument against preparation. A full battery, a paper map, a charged phone, and a plan for contacting someone are not enemies of freedom. They are what allow a person to experiment with uncertainty without making others carry the consequences.

Still, preparation can become its own form of confinement. The person who researches every restaurant, memorizes every timetable, and calculates the best route in advance may experience a trip as a series of confirmations. Unexpected things are automatically translated into problems. A closed gate is an obstacle, not an opportunity. A wrong turn is a delay, not an experience. A conversation with a stranger is an interruption, not a possible route into a larger world.

The alternative is not chaos. It is a more balanced relationship with knowledge. We can know where we are going and still leave some room for not knowing. We can use a map and also look up from it. We can respect efficiency without surrendering curiosity. We can recognize that the world contains much that cannot be reduced to our current purpose, and that not everything useful is visible from the center of our plan.

Getting lost is often described as a failure of navigation, but sometimes it is a success of imagination. It means allowing the mind to complete what the map leaves out. It permits the territory to exceed the description. It reminds us that a person can be competent, informed, and capable, and still not know everything. That combination is not a weakness to be eliminated. It is one of the conditions of being alive.

The return journey matters too. A person who has been lost may arrive at the correct place with a different sense of it. The fountain is where the map said it would be, but the person seeing it has changed. The route has included hunger, confusion, an unexpected conversation, and a few minutes in which no instruction was guiding them. The destination does not erase those minutes. It becomes part of their meaning.

Maybe this is why the wrong turn is so often worth retelling. The story is not really about the destination. It is about the moment when certainty fell away and the world reopened. We remember the embarrassment because it makes the event legible, but we also remember the light on the old wall, the stranger who pointed the way, the street that seemed impossible on paper and yet led somewhere real. The story has a lesson, though the lesson is not always “be careful.” Sometimes the lesson is simply: you did not know what was beyond the turn.

A life can have destinations without being only a sequence of arrivals. It can contain streets that were never on the plan, conversations with people we did not expect to meet, and days whose value cannot be calculated from their usefulness. To get lost is to discover that possibility, if only briefly. It is to step outside the route and discover that the world has not been waiting obediently to be crossed.

The map can go back into the drawer. The phone can be put away. And for a while, the destination can wait.

# In Praise of Getting Lost

Some of the best parts of my life have begun with a turn taken for no good reason. Not with a grand decision, not with a well-planned journey, but with a street closed, a missed turning, or the simple impulse to see what lay beyond a familiar row of buildings. I once got off a bus two stops early because the afternoon was too beautiful to spend indoors. The neighborhood was unfamiliar, the shops were shabby, and I had no idea where I was going. By dusk, I had found a tiny cinema, eaten dumplings from a place with no English sign, and watched the streetlights flicker on above a courtyard where someone was practicing the trumpet badly and happily. It was, in every practical sense, a mistake. It remains one of my favorite memories.

We are taught to regard getting lost as a failure of navigation. Maps, GPS coordinates, and turn-by-turn instructions have made wandering nearly frictionless, and we have responded by eliminating almost every opportunity to wander. We know which lane to take before leaving home. We know where to park before setting out. We know, often, how long the journey will take, how much fuel it will consume, and whether there will be traffic. Convenience is wonderful, and I do not want to return to a world in which every trip requires a paper map unfolded and refolded in the rain. Still, efficiency has a hidden cost. When we know exactly where we are going, we may arrive everywhere without having visited any of it.

Being lost and being directionless are not the same thing. The person who is lost once had a destination, or at least expected to have one. The directionless person has temporarily released the need to arrive. One is a small failure of certainty; the other can be a deliberate form of freedom. We rarely grant ourselves permission to be without an objective. We schedule our days around errands, our conversations around points, and our conversations around the possibility of future productivity. Even our rest is optimized: ten minutes of meditation, thirty minutes of walking, perhaps a carefully curated playlist intended to improve our focus. We have become skilled at going places without being there.

This is why childhood is full of getting lost. Children disappear into neighborhoods with the confidence of explorers because nobody has yet taught them to calculate the cost of a wrong turn. A backyard becomes a continent. A drainpipe is a mountain. The space behind a hedge may contain pirates, dinosaurs, a buried treasure, or a secret entrance to another world. Children do not need to make every moment meaningful. They simply encounter it, and their attention is intense enough to turn an ordinary patch of ground into a place of mystery. Somewhere along the way, adults begin correcting this. “Stay where I can see you.” “Don’t wander off.” “How did you get lost?” These phrases are usually sensible, but they gradually replace curiosity with caution.

Modern navigation makes sense of this transformation. A phone can tell us to turn left in five hundred feet, then right after passing a gas station. It can reassure us that we are still on the right path, even when the scenery is strange. At first, this feels like liberation. But a route is not the same as an experience. The map tells us the name of a street while missing the smell of bread from its basement window, the uneven rhythm of its pavement, the old woman sitting on a stoop, and the cat watching us from a wall. It tells us where to go while overlooking why we might want to go there at all. We arrive efficiently and discover that we have skipped the journey.

Perhaps this is why travel can be more memorable when something goes wrong. The planned day is pleasant, but the day the train stops, the flight is canceled, or the address cannot be found acquires a strange intensity. We notice the waiting room. We study the other passengers. We learn the particular boredom of an afternoon with nowhere to be. We notice the station café because we had never thought to enter it. Misfortunes interrupt our habit of taking the world for granted. Even inconvenience becomes a kind of tour guide, pointing out details that efficiency had made invisible.

There is a practical wisdom in the old stories about travelers who are advised to follow the path. The instruction is always the same: do not stray from the road, do not trust the shortcuts, do not be tempted by the beautiful view. The implication is that the world beyond the path is dangerous, or at least unproductive. This is useful advice when a storm is approaching or a region is unsafe. It is less useful as a philosophy of life. We may need clear paths sometimes, but the world is larger than the routes we have drawn across it. A life spent only moving from obligation to obligation can become a life spent not living at all.

To be lost is also to experience a kind of humility. We are not as in control as our plans suggest. The bus will not always arrive. The remembered shortcut may have disappeared. The person we asked for directions may not know either. In such moments, the usual hierarchy between the person who knows and the person who does not becomes briefly comic. We all become beginners again. We look up at unfamiliar signs, try to read the landscape, and ask other people what they think. Humility is often described as a spiritual virtue, but it can arrive through something as ordinary as missing a stop.

Asking for directions is one of the simplest acts of vulnerability. We must admit that we are in a place we do not understand. We must accept help from a stranger, and we must temporarily place our sense of self in someone else’s hands. The conversation is usually brief. “Excuse me, is this the road to the river?” “Keep going, then turn at the church.” The words are simple, but they create a small bridge between lives. The stranger has been here before. We have not. Their memory becomes our route, and our arrival will include them even though we may never learn their name.

There is something unexpectedly intimate about being lost in a city. The city that seemed anonymous becomes specific. We notice where people buy their lunch, which streets have trees, where the footsteps become loud, where the light from a window falls across the pavement. The city stops being a backdrop and becomes a collection of human arrangements. Every block appears to have been made by someone who wanted to solve a problem: shelter, transport, commerce, beauty, privacy, conversation. Even the neglected corners reveal intentions. The empty lot may once have been a garden. The concrete bridge may have replaced a stream. A path through a fence may have been an informal agreement between neighbors.

This is one of the great pleasures of walking without a route. A destination gives us permission to ignore everything between the beginning and the end. A journey gives us other reasons to look. We can stop at a bakery because the door is open. We can take a street because a painted door is bright red. We can sit on a bench and watch pigeons fight over a crust. These choices do not lead to productivity, but they restore attention. The world becomes less like a problem to be solved and more like a relationship to be developed. Attention, in this sense, is not a spotlight we point at things. It is a form of affection.

I have come to think that many of our deepest attachments begin as acts of attention. We love particular people not because they possess every quality, but because we have noticed how they take a cup of tea, how they become quiet when embarrassed, how they laugh before they understand the joke. We love particular landscapes because we have watched them change across years. We love songs because we have carried them through repeated circumstances until the lyrics have become part of our biography. To pay attention is to allow something to matter more than it strictly needs to. Getting lost is simply one way of making that possible.

The world is full of systems designed to prevent this kind of attention. Search engines can tell us the answer before we have formed a question. Recommendation systems can tell us what we might like before we have experienced anything new. The feed presents an endless procession of things chosen by somebody else’s model of desire. We mistake movement for discovery, and variety for curiosity. A day can contain hundreds of images without giving us one memory. We may be exposed to everything while experiencing nothing in particular. The solution is not necessarily to abandon these tools, but to remember that tools can organize our attention without supplying it.

To wander is to make a modest resistance to this condition. Not a dramatic resistance, not a withdrawal from the world, but a willingness to be unguided for an afternoon. Take the long street. Walk without counting the minutes. Choose the market instead of the station. Sit somewhere you have never sat. Let the route depend on weather, conversation, or a change of mind. There is no need to turn wandering into a spiritual practice or a personality trait. Its value may be simpler: it reminds us that time can be spent without being spent on something else.

The best walks are often the ones that achieve nothing. We return home with no souvenir, no photograph, and no particularly useful story. Yet something has shifted. A street we had ignored has become a place we know. A mistake has revealed a preference. A period of uncertainty has allowed an idea to surface that would otherwise have remained buried. Sometimes we need to stop answering the question “How do I get there?” in order to ask the more interesting question, “What becomes possible when I am not on my way?”

This does not mean that uncertainty is always beneficial. A person lost in a dangerous place may need help, and a person who is driving through a snowstorm should not treat navigation as an experiment. The celebration of wandering becomes irresponsible if it ignores real differences in safety and privilege. Not everyone can afford to miss a train, wander away from a support system, or follow an unexplained path. To speak freely about getting lost is also to recognize that most of us are surrounded by maps, resources, and directions that others may not have.

Even within those limits, however, we can practice small uncertainties. Read a book without rushing toward its conclusion. Walk through a familiar park by a route you have never chosen. Allow a conversation to continue without steering it toward an objective. Learn the name of a street merely because you have crossed it many times without knowing what it was called. These acts are tiny, almost invisible. They are not escapes from responsibility. They are ways of remembering that a life is not solely a sequence of completed objectives.

There is also a form of getting lost that has nothing to do with geography. We can lose ourselves in a book, a piece of music, a conversation, or an idea. The world may continue outside, but for a while we do not notice it. The hours pass. The body remains seated, while the mind travels elsewhere. This kind of disappearance is one of the reasons stories matter. Fiction gives us permission to inhabit lives that are not ours, to cross borders without passports, to experience losses and victories that belong to other people. A good novel does not confuse us about reality. It enlarges reality by showing us how many other ways of seeing it might exist.

Children often seem naturally capable of this kind of imaginative travel. They do not require a plot to explain why they are spending time with a cardboard box. The box can be a boat, a house, a hospital, or a machine for traveling to the moon. Their boredom is not empty. It is the space in which invention begins. It may look like nothing from the outside: a child sitting alone, moving a small object across the floor. Inside, the room has become a theater. We should be careful not to romanticize childhood or hold adults to impossible standards, but we can remember that boredom is not always a problem requiring immediate correction.

We often rush to fill every pause because silence makes us uncomfortable. We reach for our phones before the elevator arrives. We turn on the radio in the car even when we do not need company. We seek constant stimulation as though stillness were a warning. Yet the mind, given a little room, may produce its own material. It may remember a forgotten conversation, notice a pattern in ordinary events, or construct a plan for something we had believed impossible. The empty moment is not necessarily unproductive. It may be where the next thought enters.

A garden offers a useful example. If we plant seeds and then check them every minute, we may disturb the process. We can water them, protect them, and make sure they receive light, but we must also wait. The waiting is part of the relationship. We cannot force a flower to bloom by staring at its stem. In the same way, certain parts of our inner lives develop at their own pace. We may not know what we are becoming until the conditions are right. Aimlessness, properly understood, is not the same as giving up. It is allowing growth to exceed the timetable we imagined for it.

The phrase “lost in translation” suggests another kind of dislocation. We may lose a word, a joke, an emotion, or a piece of our own history. Language fails us. The sentence we had carefully prepared comes out differently in another language. The explanation we expected to clarify a misunderstanding instead makes it worse. We lose the path back to what we meant. Yet the awkwardness can be productive. When words stop working perfectly, we begin to notice tone, gesture, context, and silence. Translation becomes an act of interpretation rather than substitution. We discover that meaning is not a package that can be carried unchanged from one person to another.

A similar thing happens in music when a melody is separated from its lyrics. We know a tune that once carried one meaning, and now it belongs to a different room, a different year, a different person. The song is still recognizable, but the feeling has changed. Memory is not an archive. It is an ongoing arrangement. We may lose the original context, but we do not lose the experience of having known it. Sometimes the meaning that remains is stranger and more valuable than the meaning we first assigned.

To be lost is therefore to encounter the limits of certainty. We are always interpreting the world, and every interpretation may be partial. The route we have drawn is one route among many. The story we tell about our lives is one story among several. The person we believe ourselves to be may change when circumstances force us to choose a different street. This can be unsettling, but it can also be liberating. We are not obligated to remain faithful to every earlier version of ourselves.

One of the great reliefs of wandering is that it does not demand a performance. There is no need to look impressive, knowledgeable, or efficient. We may walk slowly. We may ask a child to point out the way. We may admit that we have no idea what happens at the end of the road. When we are not trying to impress anyone, our relation to the place becomes more honest. We can be interested without pretending to understand. We can be delighted by something without immediately knowing whether it is useful. Wonder is a form of knowledge, though not the kind that can be entered into a spreadsheet.

Many people describe travel as a way of finding themselves. Sometimes that is true, but I prefer to think of it as a way of finding out how many selves are possible. A person may be confident in one environment and hesitant in another. One city may bring out our sociability; another may bring out our patience. A solitary week may reveal a capacity for solitude we did not know we possessed. A crowded journey may teach us that companionship can exist without constant conversation. We do not discover a fixed essence. We discover that we can change shape without losing continuity.

I have met people whose stories begin with an accidental detour. They took a wrong train and found the town where they later studied art. They missed the last bus and met the friend who changed their career. They wandered into a lecture instead of a lecture and discovered a subject they now love. These stories can sound like fate in retrospect, but at the time they probably felt like inconvenience. The lesson is not that every mistake is a blessing. It is that a mistake does not have to be wasted.

Perhaps this is why the best stories rarely begin with perfect preparation. They begin with a disruption: a letter arrives unexpectedly, a stranger overhears something, a storm prevents a departure. The disruption makes room for a different future. If everything goes according to plan, the future may simply repeat the present. A little confusion gives the world an opening. It creates a space in which something unforeseen can enter. The person who never gets lost may never feel this opening, but neither may the person who uses getting lost as a way of avoiding responsibility. The gift lies not in confusion itself, but in what we do with it.

Our maps are useful for certain journeys, and our plans are useful for certain days. But we should not confuse them with the territory of a life. A map can show the river, but it cannot feel the water. It can show the mountain, but it cannot describe the relief of reaching the summit or the disappointment of arriving at the wrong one. The plan can provide structure, but it cannot tell us what the weather will do to our expectations. There must be room for the uncharted, even if the uncharted is only a few unfamiliar streets.

This is why I distrust the fantasy of a life fully known in advance. Such a fantasy sounds like freedom from uncertainty, but it is really freedom from surprise. It removes the possibility of being pleasantly interrupted. It makes every choice predictable and every day an extension of the day before. A little uncertainty is what keeps the future open. It keeps the world from becoming a closed system of obligations we have already agreed to perform. The detour is not always a deviation from the path. Sometimes it is the path itself.

In the evening, when I return from a walk without having intended to return, I often feel that I have crossed a border. Familiar streets have become briefly unfamiliar. I notice the moon between two buildings, the shape of a shadow, the sound of a bicycle chain. For a moment, the world seems to have rearranged itself while I was absent. Nothing has actually changed, except the arrangement of my attention. The walk has made the ordinary strange again.

I do not mean that ordinary life should be permanently strange. We need houses, schedules, meals, and people who can find us when we are needed. We need enough certainty to keep promises and enough structure to accomplish difficult things. But a life needs a little uncertainty to remain alive to possibility. Otherwise we may be so busy preserving our plans that we fail to notice the life happening around us.

When I put my phone away and walk without a destination, the effect is modest. I do not become wiser. I do not achieve enlightenment. I may still be hungry, late, or wearing the wrong shoes. But I return with a more vivid sense of the place. The world has been there all along, waiting to be noticed. Its details have not been waiting for me specifically, exactly. Yet attention makes them available. To pay attention is to discover that reality has been generously furnished for a great many people, and that we have only begun to look.

There is a particular freedom in not knowing which turn comes next. It releases us from the expectation that every choice must lead somewhere important. We can take the long way simply because it is long. We can sit beside a fountain without calculating how many minutes remain before we must leave. We can look at a blank wall and allow it to be blank. In a culture organized around acceleration, this freedom may seem almost subversive. It asks nothing of us except that we stop treating every moment as an opportunity to advance.

Over time, these small departures accumulate. They become a private geography, a map made not of destinations but of experiences. The street where someone gave us directions. The bench where we watched a summer storm. The bakery where the baker remembered our order. The path we found by accident and have returned to ever since. This map is invisible to anyone else, and that is part of its value. It records a relationship between a person and a place, not simply a sequence of coordinates.

The final pleasure of getting lost is that the return can feel like an arrival. We come back to familiar rooms, but they are not exactly as we left them. We have changed by a fraction. The world has changed by a fraction. Even if the street is still there and the bus still passes at the same time, the person crossing the threshold has been somewhere else. A walk without a destination may therefore return us to the destination differently. We are not lost forever. We are only reminded that being found is not the same as being finished.

In the end, I hope we can keep a little room in our lives for the wrong turn, the unasked street, the afternoon without an objective. Not as a form of carelessness, but as a form of openness. Not because the world needs us to be lost, but because we need the world to remain larger than our plan for it. A map is a useful companion. It can help us find our way and teach us where we are. But occasionally we should put it away, look up, and allow the unknown to become—not a threat, not a test, but an invitation.
